name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,747

clue.text: Wicked dance beat one put on in America?

blocks.note: base means low or morally wicked
a ball is a formal dance
to cap something is to top or beat it

explanation.surface: A wild dance track has been released for the American market.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: 'one put on' is something you put on your head, and the question mark and 'in America' point to the headgear of America's national game.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the peaked hat Americans typically wear, a garment you put on, clued vaguely with a hint of location.

clue.text: Bosoms filled by doctor finally popped

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter of the word is kept
something filled by something else has it placed inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a woman's bust is her bosoms
the last letter of doctor

explanation.surface: A slightly saucy picture of a doctor's final act popping something.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes into the middle of BUST, between U and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has burst has broken open suddenly, just as a balloon that popped has split apart.

clue.text: Juicy cut uncle munched after drop of sangria

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount, so only the first letter of the word is taken
food that is munched is chewed up and broken apart, so the letters are mashed into a new order

blocks.note: the first letter of sangria
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An uncle enjoys a juicy cut of meat after a drop of sangria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the rearranged letters behind S. 'Juicy cut' reads as one phrase about meat, but 'Juicy' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Succulent food is tender and full of juice, so the two adjectives are close synonyms.

clue.text: Black dog eats half of room with Egyptian fabric

indicators.note: what eats something takes it inside, so one piece swallows another

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
the first half of the four-letter word room
a dog in the sense of a rotter or scoundrel is a cad
E is an abbreviation for Egyptian, as in E£ for the Egyptian pound

explanation.surface: A black dog chews up part of a room and some expensive Egyptian cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black dog' works as one unit that does the eating, so the room fragment lands after its first letter. 'Egyptian fabric' looks like a single phrase, but only 'fabric' defines; E£ is the Egyptian pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Brocade is a rich woven textile with a raised pattern, often in gold or silver thread, a kind of cloth.

clue.text: Fat relations have a whale of a time

definitions.text: have a whale of a time

blocks.note: fat and large both mean big in size
IT is a euphemism for sex, and relations means sexual relations

explanation.surface: Plump relatives enjoying themselves enormously at a family party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relations' suggests family, but here it means sexual relations, a sense crosswords often render as IT. 'Large it' is British slang for partying hard.
explanation.definitionFit: To large it is British slang for going out and partying wildly, the same as having enormous fun on a night out.

clue.text: One who thought uni grounds not quiet?

indicators.note: not means without, so the following letter is taken out

blocks.note: a university's grounds are its campus
P is piano, the musical instruction to play quietly

explanation.surface: Someone who assumed the university grounds would be noisy.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove P from CAMPUS. Albert Camus was the French writer and philosopher of the absurd, fittingly clued as a thinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Camus was a celebrated philosopher, and a philosopher is literally a person whose work is thinking.

clue.text: Simple little Barney is one seen in court

blocks.note: simple and plain both mean unadorned
a barney is British slang for a quarrel, and a small one is a tiff

explanation.surface: A simple fellow called Barney ends up appearing in court.
explanation.walkthrough: Barney looks like a man's name; it is British slang for a row or argument, and a little row is a tiff.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaintiff brings a legal case against someone, so is a party regularly present at a court hearing.

clue.text: Knight loves to hug colt with constant wind

indicators.note: hugging something means wrapping arms around it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a knight has the title Sir
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O; two of them
c is the abbreviation for colt in horse racing
c is the constant for the speed of light

explanation.surface: An affectionate knight hugs his young horse in a relentless wind.
explanation.walkthrough: The two O's wrap around the pair of C's, all after SIR.
explanation.definitionFit: The sirocco is a hot dusty wind blowing from North Africa across the Mediterranean into southern Europe.

clue.text: One that shoots driver in wild armed escape

indicators.note: something wild is out of control, so the letters run loose into another order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A gunman shoots a getaway driver during a wild armed escape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoots' suggests a gun, fitting the armed escape, but a camera shoots too: it photographs the speeding driver.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadside speed camera photographs, or shoots, motorists who break the limit, catching the driver on film.

clue.text: Hit rubbish tenor, being violent in behaviour

blocks.note: to ram is to strike hard
to rubbish something is to criticise it harshly, or pan it
T is the abbreviation for tenor

explanation.surface: A critic attacks a poor tenor for his aggressive behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish' reads as a noun describing the tenor, but it is a verb meaning to criticise scathingly.
explanation.definitionFit: Rampant describes behaviour that is wild, unrestrained and aggressive, like a rearing lion on a coat of arms.

clue.text: He hated Tory changes in the recent past

indicators.note: changes means alters, so the letters are altered into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man disliked the changes the Conservatives brought in lately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changes' looks like a noun, the thing he hated, but it is a verb acting on the preceding words. A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a few days ago, an unspecified recent time, so it works as an adverbial for recently.

clue.text: Urge at one to get all sorts of wrong with escort

indicators.note: something all sorts of wrong is thoroughly messed up, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lone impulse to go very badly astray alongside a paid companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Escort' suggests a single companion, but it can also be a group accompanying someone important.
explanation.definitionFit: An entourage is the group of attendants accompanying a celebrity or dignitary, which is an escort in the collective sense.

clue.text: Feeling nurse gets aboard ship with European

indicators.note: someone aboard a vessel is inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: EN is Enrolled Nurse
SS is steamship
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A nurse boards a ship with a European companion and has a feeling about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets aboard ship' is nautical in the surface and literal in the wordplay: the nurse really does go inside the ship abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A sense is a feeling or perception, as in a sense of dread or a sense of unease.

clue.text: My boss rejected Friends of the Earth writer

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters go backwards

blocks.note: a setter's boss is the editor, ED
FOE is the initialism of the environmental group

explanation.surface: An editor turns down a piece by a green campaigning author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My boss' is the setter speaking: a crossword setter answers to the editor. Daniel Defoe wrote Robinson Crusoe.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel Defoe was an English novelist and journalist, author of Robinson Crusoe and Moll Flanders.

clue.text: Shoot a large gun to provide a warning?

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the device whose purpose is warning

blocks.note: to shoot a gun is to fire it
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for large
a gun is a firearm, or arm

explanation.surface: Firing a big gun into the air as a warning shot.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: the answer is a thing, while the clue describes what it does.
explanation.definitionFit: A fire alarm is a bell or siren whose purpose is to alert people to danger in a building.

clue.text: Old lover very tense around Michigan radical

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece is wrapped about another

blocks.note: a former partner is an ex
très is French for very
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
MI is the postal abbreviation for Michigan

explanation.surface: A nervous former partner is now a Michigan political firebrand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very tense' reads as a description of the old lover, but it is two pieces joined, French for very plus the tense abbreviation, which together wrap round the state.
explanation.definitionFit: A radical and an extremist both hold views far from the political mainstream and favour drastic change.

clue.text: Discerning flapper Hoskins had picked up

indicators.note: to pick something up is to catch it by ear, so the sound matters rather than spelling

blocks.note: a flapper is something that flaps its wings, like an eagle
Hoskins is the setter, so the setter had is I had, contracted

explanation.surface: A shrewd 1920s flapper girl the setter once dated.
explanation.walkthrough: A flapper suggests a 1920s party girl; here it is a bird flapping its wings. The setter refers to himself by name, so 'Hoskins had' is I'D.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with sharp eyesight notices every detail, so being keen-sighted is the same as being perceptive and observant.

clue.text: Hoskins will punch a smarter criminal with wind

indicators.note: criminal means crooked or wrong, so the letters are bent into a new order
a punch goes into something, so one piece is driven inside another

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
Hoskins is the setter, who is I

explanation.surface: The setter threatens to hit a cleverer crook who is full of hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter uses his own name for I, which goes after the first letter of the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An airstream is a current or flow of air, and wind is moving air, so they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Former idea about independence? I need more info!

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: ex- means former
an idea or scheme is a plan
I is the abbreviation for independence or independent

explanation.surface: Someone baffled by an old notion about independence demands clarification.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an exclamation: the answer is exactly what a confused listener would say.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'Explain!' is an imperative demand for clarification, the same thing as announcing you want further details.

clue.text: Chap on escort getting instruction

blocks.note: a chap is a man
someone's escort for the evening is their date

explanation.surface: A man working as an escort receives his orders.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandate is an official order or authorisation to act, so it is a formal kind of command.

clue.text: Manager missing the final could be a blunder

indicators.note: missing the final means lacking the end, so the closing letter is dropped

blocks.note: British slang for a boss, especially a football manager

explanation.surface: A football manager whose team fails to reach the cup final has made a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The final' sounds like a cup final; it means the last letter. Gaffer is British slang for a boss or football manager.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaffe is a social or diplomatic slip, an embarrassing mistake, which is what a blunder is.

clue.text: Precise English bit of play will defend cross

indicators.note: defenders surround what they protect, so one piece is shielded inside another

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
an act is a section of a play
a cross is the shape X

explanation.surface: A precise English footballer's play defends a cross into the box.
explanation.walkthrough: E and ACT together defend X, which sits between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Exact and precise both mean accurate in every detail, with no error or approximation.

clue.text: You might say all the best will be certain to die

definitions.text: You might say all the best

blocks.clueFragment: You might say all the best
blocks.note: first meaning: a drink raised with good wishes to someone
second meaning: slang for doomed, finished

explanation.surface: Wishing everyone the best as they face certain death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You might say' suggests a sound-alike, but it just introduces what you say when raising a glass. 'You're toast' means you are done for.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising a glass with good wishes is proposing a toast, and in slang someone doomed is described as toast.

clue.text: Bound to get on flipping drink to get stupid

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: a nip is a small drink of spirits
bound for a place is headed for it

explanation.surface: Someone certain to carry on with a blasted drink until they are senseless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British expletive, but it turns the drink round. 'Get on' places HEADED after the reversed drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinheaded is an informal insult meaning brainless, implying a head as small as a pin's, hence stupid.

clue.text: Republican into Barbie perhaps? That's oddly amusing!

indicators.note: into means going inside, so one piece enters another

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican
Barbie is an example of a doll

explanation.surface: A Republican who is a fan of the Barbie film: how peculiar and funny!
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Barbie the film, but here it is the toy, and 'perhaps' marks it as an example. 'Oddly' reads as an adverb for the exclamation but belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Droll humour is dry and whimsical, amusing in a quirky, curious way rather than broadly comic.

clue.text: A mother, after advanced labour, is a state

indicators.note: after means following, so the pieces named before this word are placed behind those named after it

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for advanced, as in A level
Lab is the short form of the Labour Party
taken as written
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A mother late in labour is in quite a state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advanced labour' suggests childbirth; it is A plus LAB, for Britain's Labour Party. 'After' puts 'A mother' behind them. 'A state' pretends to mean a flustered condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Alabama is one of the fifty United States, in the American South, so it is an example of a state.

clue.text: An important type in a foreign city council?

blocks.note: taken as written
NY is New York, a city abroad from a British viewpoint
a council is a governing body

explanation.surface: A dignitary sitting on a city council overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer means a person of some importance, as in 'everybody who is anybody'.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a noun, the word denotes someone of note or status, as in asking whether a person is anybody in society.

clue.text: Note I’m ideal to be cast as a handsome actor

indicators.note: cast means thrown or moulded, so the letters are thrown into a new shape

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A note from someone who thinks he is perfect for a heartthrob role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' fits the theatrical surface, where actors are cast in roles, but here it signals the letters being thrown into new order.
explanation.definitionFit: A matinee idol is a good-looking actor adored by fans, originally stars of afternoon film and theatre showings.
